Pregnancy

Elderberry in pregnancy: evidence, preparation and safety

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Elderberry is marketed for colds and flu, but there is not enough pregnancy-specific evidence to recommend it as a remedy. The practical questions are which plant and product you mean, what the research actually measured, and whether symptoms need established treatment. Natural origin and cooking do not settle all of these questions.

What counts as elderberry?

Most research concerns black or European elder, Sambucus nigra, and particular fruit extracts. Elderflower, leaves, bark and stems are different plant parts; a common name or a similar-looking berry does not identify a safe substitute. Do not identify a foraged plant from a supplement photograph.

Elderberry has a long history of medicinal use. That history explains its popularity but does not demonstrate safety for a developing baby. A cooked food, a concentrated extract and a mixed herbal tea also represent different exposures.

Pregnancy safety remains uncertain

Human evidence is insufficient to establish the safety of medicinal elderberry during pregnancy. NIH guidance recommends against elderberry supplements in pregnancy because safety is unknown. Do not start a syrup, capsule, gummy or medicinal tea for prevention or treatment without discussing the exact product and your symptoms with your maternity clinician or pharmacist.

This uncertainty is not proof that a single accidental dose has harmed a pregnancy. It also does not establish a safe trimester, dose or treatment duration. A clinician’s product review can guide the next step; it cannot turn missing pregnancy studies into a guarantee. Breastfeeding information is limited too.

What the 2016 and 2019 reports actually found

A 2016 randomized trial analyzed 312 air travellers. Only 29 developed a defined cold; fewer colds occurred with elderberry, but the difference was not statistically significant. Among those who became ill, duration and symptom scores were lower. Pregnant, breastfeeding and pregnancy-planning participants were excluded. This was not a pregnancy trial or proof that elderberry prevents infection.

The 2019 report was a meta-analysis of four small trials, with 180 participants in its pooled symptom analysis, rather than one new clinical trial. It reported favorable respiratory symptom results. However, a 2020 trial in 87 influenza patients found no overall benefit, and a 2021 systematic review judged the evidence uncertain. Different products and populations limit generalization; none establishes a pregnancy benefit or fetal safety.

Traditional uses are not proven indications

Traditional claims include upper respiratory symptoms, toothache, sinus problems, flu-like headache, sciatica, hay fever, chronic fatigue and constipation. Evidence is insufficient to treat this list as established elderberry benefits. Laboratory antiviral or immune effects are not the same as recovery in a pregnant person.

Treat the underlying problem rather than choosing elderberry because it is described as multipurpose. Toothache may need dental care; persistent or worsening symptoms need assessment. Do not replace prescribed treatment or use a supplement to postpone checking a possible infection.

Raw fruit and other plant parts can cause illness

Raw or unripe elderberries and parts such as leaves, stems and bark can contain cyanide-producing compounds and cause nausea, vomiting or diarrhea; serious poisoning is possible. Lectins have also been identified in elder fruit or seeds, but listing two chemicals does not predict the risk of a particular homemade preparation.

Avoid raw berries, uncertain plant identification and preparations containing unsuitable plant parts. Persistent vomiting or diarrhea can cause dehydration. A photograph of berries and leaves illustrates the plant; it is not advice to eat the pictured parts.

Why a homemade syrup is not a pregnancy safety solution

Appropriate cooking or processing addresses the cyanogenic toxin concern. It does not establish pregnancy safety, a therapeutic dose or effectiveness. Some internet recipes may not use adequate preparation methods, and adding sugar does not itself detoxify a plant.

Do not use a home recipe as a validated way to make a pregnancy remedy, including a recipe starting with dried berries. Species, plant parts and processing matter. Properly prepared food is not equivalent to a concentrated medicinal course, but this distinction does not supply a measured pregnancy-safe amount here.

Commercial forms need individual checking

Syrups, teas, powders, capsules, lozenges and gummies vary in concentration and ingredients. A fruit extract is not interchangeable with an elderflower blend. Commercial manufacture does not establish pregnancy safety, and US dietary supplements are not FDA-approved for safety and effectiveness before sale.

Bring the complete label, including other herbs, vitamins and sweeteners. Discuss regular medicines, diabetes and immune-suppressing treatment: potential effects on glucose or drug action need individual review, not an assumption that every interaction is proven. Do not combine several “immune” products or stop prescribed medicine to make room for one.

If you have already taken some

Stop further nonessential elderberry use while you obtain product-specific advice. Record the name, ingredients, amount, time, pregnancy stage and symptoms. An incidental exposure alone cannot establish either fetal harm or complete safety; your care team can decide whether any follow-up is warranted.

For raw or unidentified berries, unsuitable plant parts, an overdose or suspected poisoning, contact an urgent medical or poison service immediately; do not wait for symptoms. If you think a harmful substance was swallowed, seek emergency assessment. Do not induce vomiting or give food or drink unless the poison or emergency team directs it. Keep the container or plant information for assessment.

Cold and flu symptoms deserve an appropriate plan

For a straightforward cold, rest and enough fluids can help with comfort. Ask about pregnancy-compatible symptom treatment; paracetamol/acetaminophen may be appropriate for pain or fever when used as directed. Have combination cold products checked, because ingredients differ and may duplicate medicines or contain a decongestant.

If you suspect flu, contact your clinician promptly rather than trying elderberry first. Pregnancy increases the risk of complications. Antiviral treatment may be started without waiting for test confirmation; it works best early, but later presentation is still a reason to seek care. Elderberry is not a substitute for recommended vaccination or prescribed antiviral treatment.

When to seek urgent help

Call emergency services for loss of consciousness, a seizure, severe breathing difficulty or stopped breathing. Do not drive yourself; ask someone to drive or call an ambulance. Suspected poisoning needs immediate assessment even before symptoms develop. You do not need several warning signs together.

During pregnancy, seek immediate medical assessment for fever of 38°C or higher, new breathing difficulty, chest pain, fainting or persistent dizziness, inability to keep fluids down, or severe abdominal pain that starts suddenly, persists or worsens. Contact maternity care immediately for reduced or stopped fetal movement when movements are established. Do not dismiss these as an expected reaction to a natural product.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Review the exact plant part, formulation and ingredients rather than treating all elderberry products as equivalent.

Do not extrapolate respiratory symptom results in nonpregnant people into pregnancy safety or efficacy.

How BeMama can help

Keep a photograph of the label and a short list of symptoms and medicines, so a pharmacist or maternity clinician can advise on the actual exposure and a suitable treatment plan.

When to seek help

Seek immediate advice for raw or uncertain plant ingestion, overdose or suspected poisoning; do not wait for symptoms or induce vomiting. Suspected harmful ingestion requires emergency assessment. Call emergency services for unconsciousness, seizure, severe breathing difficulty or stopped breathing; do not drive yourself. Pregnancy fever of 38°C or more, new breathing difficulty, chest pain, fainting or persistent dizziness, inability to keep fluids down, sudden severe, persistent or worsening abdominal pain, or reduced fetal movement needs immediate medical or maternity assessment.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Pregnancy safety and an effective pregnancy dose of elderberry are not established.
  • Small nonpregnant respiratory studies have mixed results and cannot establish fetal safety.
  • Raw or unripe berries and unsuitable plant parts can cause poisoning.
  • Cooking and commercial manufacture do not guarantee a pregnancy-safe remedy.
  • Suspected poisoning or flu calls for appropriate medical care, not another supplement dose.

Frequently asked questions

Is elderberry safe during pregnancy?

There is not enough evidence to recommend medicinal use. Avoid self-starting supplements and review the exact product with your maternity clinician or pharmacist; no safe pregnancy dose has been established.

Does cooking make it safe?

Appropriate processing addresses the cyanogenic toxin, but does not prove pregnancy safety or effectiveness. A homemade recipe is not a validated pregnancy treatment.

Are gummies or commercial syrup safer?

They differ from raw plant material, but formulation, other ingredients and pregnancy evidence still matter. A commercial label is not a pregnancy safety guarantee.

Can it cure a cold or flu?

Some small studies suggested shorter symptoms, while others found no benefit. The evidence is uncertain and does not establish a pregnancy treatment. Suspected flu needs prompt clinical advice.

Are the other traditional benefits established?

No. Claims about toothache, sinus symptoms, headache, sciatica, hay fever, fatigue or constipation are not proven pregnancy indications. Assess and treat the actual problem.

What if I already had one dose?

Do not assume harm or complete safety. Keep the label and record the amount and time, then obtain individual advice. Raw or uncertain plant exposure, overdose or suspected poisoning needs immediate poison or medical advice without waiting for symptoms.

Can I make syrup from dried berries?

Dried berries are not a validated pregnancy remedy. Identity, plant parts and processing still matter, and no home recipe establishes a safe dose or benefit.

Which symptoms need help now?

Suspected poisoning needs immediate assessment. Call emergency services for unconsciousness, a seizure, severe breathing difficulty or stopped breathing; do not drive yourself. In pregnancy, fever of 38°C or more, breathing difficulty, chest pain, fainting or persistent dizziness, fluid intolerance, sudden severe, persistent or worsening abdominal pain, or reduced fetal movement needs immediate medical or maternity assessment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
